TESTING LESSON (2026-08-26, cost 3 real defects in one session):

A test that asserts what was WRITTEN passes while the thing that should HAPPEN
doesn't. Three findings this session, three subsystems, one root cause:

1. PR #1489 — "declining hands the lock back to its real provider" shipped with
   the handing-back not happening until a restart. The test asserted the stored
   `members` dict. `_async_apply_entry_update` only churns provider instances on
   roster changes and never consults `members`, so at runtime the lock was still
   a CodelessLock. Fully green.
2. PR #1487 — calendar_condition docs promised a template referencing the removed
   `lock_entity_ids` "fails loudly, sensor goes unavailable". Reproduced: sensor
   reads `off`, stays available, PIN silently never activates. The reasoning about
   Jinja was plausible and wrong; nobody had rendered it.
3. PR #1489 — an error string told users to "go back and let LCM hold the codes".
   HA forms have no back button, and the answer is cached for the life of the
   flow. The copy described an affordance that does not exist.

Mutation discipline CANNOT catch class 1: mutating the storage code correctly
kills the storage test. The test is testing the right thing at the wrong layer.
What caught all three was running the scenario and looking at the result —
`runtime_data.locks[...]`, the rendered sensor state, the actual flow screens.

RULE: for any claim of the form "X causes Y", the test must observe Y. If Y is a
provider class, assert the class. If Y is a rendered state, render it. If Y is
what a user sees, drive the flow.

DESIGN ARC 2026-08-26 — issue #1414 (ESPHome keypad support) → the credential-store model.

Four designs, each smaller than the last, each cut by Raman pushing back. Final
surface answers the original request as well as the first one did.

1. CREDENTIAL READER PROVIDER — a sensor/text keypad entity added to CONF_LOCKS
   via a new config-flow field, subscribed to and validated automatically. Built,
   reviewed, then CUT: ~2/3 of the diff for a benefit of ~4 lines in an automation
   the user writes anyway (LCM never actuates). Preserved on branch
   `reader-provider-full`.
2. validate_code with lock attribution — cut. Attributing a keypad use to a lock
   is a fiction, and firing at a lock whose provider lacks supports_code_slot_events
   (Akuvox, Schlage, Virtual — this feature's actual users) raised inside the
   event handler.
3. validate_code as a pure query — superseded.
4. use_credential + unified event — SHIPPED in 5.2.0.

WHY THE PROVIDER WAS THE WRONG SHAPE: it anchored on an entity whose STATE WAS A
PIN. All four disclosure bugs came from that single property — dashboard badge,
one-click more-info dialog (with history graph), the success event republishing
it via ATTR_STATE into the recorder, and diagnostics bundles. A lock-domain anchor
(state = locked/unlocked) makes all four structurally impossible. That is why
#1484 (codeless locks) is the safe version of the same shape.

RAMAN'S REFRAME that reorganised everything: "VirtualLock really should be
VirtualKeypad — the lock itself doesn't matter." Correct, and stronger than
stated: LCM never reads ANY provider's lock state, only availability and
friendly_name. "Lock" conflates three things that coincide only on a real lock —
the credential STORE, the ENTRY POINT, and the ACTUATED thing. The event already
separates the last two (source/target); the store is the piece still called a lock.

DECISIONS THAT HELD:
- LCM never actuates. An actuate_if_valid field was designed and cancelled: no
  vocabulary generalises across lock/cover/light/vacuum. A blueprint's action
  selector covers all of them with zero domain knowledge in the integration.
- Declaration beats platform dispatch. Once a user says "LCM holds these codes",
  a future release adding a provider for that platform must not silently start
  writing PINs to their door.
- source and target are both REQUIRED on the event, with documented escape
  hatches (virtual lock as target, template entity as source). An optional field
  pushes a conditional into every consumer forever; a required one pushes one
  setup step onto the few producers that lack a natural entity.

WORKING WITH RAMAN — reinforced 2026-08-26 across a long multi-PR session.

"FEELS OVERCOMPLICATED" IS A DEFECT REPORT, AND HE IS RIGHT FROM LESS DETAIL THAN
I HAVE. Four times this session he cut something I had built and reviewed:
- "Is there a better design that's easier to maintain for users?" → killed a
  provider that was 2/3 of the diff.
- "Why are we trying to force attribution?" → killed the lock_entity_id field.
- "What is the value of the success event? If the service returns a response, is
  the event even needed?" → killed both event paths, leaving a pure query.
- "Let's get rid of this actuation feature." → replaced an enumerated verb
  vocabulary with a blueprint action selector, which covers strictly more.
Each time the capability stayed the same or grew while the integration shrank.
Pattern in my failures: I put the knowledge INSIDE the integration (a provider
that understood keypads, an event that guessed attribution, a vocabulary that
enumerated domains). Each replacement moved it to whoever actually has it.

HE ASKS FOR BREVITY AND MEANS IT. "Make the PR descriptions readable, they are so
long!" and "try to be brief instead of just additive, you've already provided a
lot of info that is hard to consume." When updating issues, REWRITE the body
rather than appending comments; delete superseded comments. Keep reasoning that
changes a decision; cut the narrative of how we got there.

PROCESS PREFERENCES CONFIRMED:
- Worktree per task, subagent per task, review every PR — every review round this
  session found something real.
- "Don't merge anything without my explicit say so." He merges; I prepare.
- Integration branch for a multi-PR arc, PRs retargeted onto it. NOTE: CI only
  triggered on PRs to main — had to widen integration.yaml's branch filter, or
  the whole arc would have merged CI-unverified.

MY WORST MISTAKE THIS SESSION: ran `git checkout main` in the MAIN checkout while
another session was working on `fix/config-flow-field-labels`. Restored intact,
nothing lost. A subagent did the same class of thing earlier by trusting cwd.
Absolute paths, always, when worktrees exist — and never switch branches in a
checkout I did not create.

### Finding

`custom_components/lock_code_manager/config_flow.py:1236` — Options-flow decline on an unloaded entry orphans the codeless credential store (cleartext PINs) permanently.

The options flow keeps `codeless_reconsider`'s stated promise ("the codes Lock Code Manager was holding for it are discarded") only via the update listener → `_async_locks_redeclared` → `locks_to_remove` → `async_unload_lock(remove_permanently=True)`. That listener is unregistered whenever the entry is not `LOADED`. Confirmed by test: put the entry in `SETUP_ERROR`, open Options, decline the reconsider — `members: {}` is written, nothing tears the provider down, and after a subsequent successful reload (member now resolves to its real provider) `hass_storage['codeless_lock_code_manager_lock.test_1']` still holds `{'1': {'code': '9999', ...}}` with nothing left that will ever read or sweep it. The reauth path already has `_async_discard_reclaimed_credentials` for precisely this reason (line 1099); the options path assumes the listener always runs. The same gap orphans the store when a codeless lock is simply *dropped* from the roster via the options flow while the entry is unloaded — adjacent to the known #1491, but a different trigger (options, not reauth).

### Hypotheses I chased and cleared

- **Per-lock entity churn on redeclaration.** A redeclared lock lands in both `locks_to_add` and `locks_to_remove`, and per-lock entity removal is a *scheduled task*, not awaited — I expected a duplicate-unique-ID collision or the stale entity's `ent_reg.async_remove(self.entity_id)` deleting the freshly re-added row. Probed it: removal completes before the add, entities come back with correct state, no warnings.
- **`BaseLock.__eq__`/`__hash__` removal.** No remaining code puts providers in sets/dicts keyed by value; `get_locks_from_targets` already dedupes by entity id before building its list.
- **Fresh `CodelessLock` reporting empty occupancy** (`_data` is `{}` on a borrowed instance that never ran `async_setup`). Harmless: `Occupancy.claimed_by_other_entries` covers every slot another entry holds, and for a codeless lock all occupied slots are LCM-managed.
- **Disabled sibling losing its shared store** on entry deletion — `_lock_managed_by_other_entry` uses `include_disabled=False` while `_sibling_declarations` deliberately includes disabled entries. Real asymmetry, but probed and self-healing: re-enabling resyncs the PIN from the entry config. Not reported.
- **Two entries diverging on one lock** (sibling adopts a different-class instance → teardown/rebuild loop on every save). Only reachable from hand-edited `.storage`; `codeless_conflict` makes it unrepresentable through every flow.
- Error-key moves (`base` → `users`/`unregistered_locks`), placeholder collisions, `assert lock_entry` reachability, `_declared_members` pruning, MRO/`__init__` chaining for the mixin, and provider dataclass construction in the deletion sweep — all check out.

## Decisions

**Field name: `lock_entity_id`.** Two sibling actions (`set_usercode`, `clear_usercode`) already spell "the lock entity this action is about" exactly that way with a `domain: lock` selector; a third spelling would make the catalog inconsistent. (`EntryConfig.member()` argues the roster is really "members", not "locks", but the roster key, `has_lock`, and every existing service field are lock-named — changing that vocabulary is a separate job.)

**Both supplied → schema error.** `lock_entity_id` joins `config_entry_id`/`config_entry_title` in the *same* `vol.Exclusive` group, with `has_at_least_one_key` across all three. The lock is a third way to *name the entry*, not an extra filter — the entry it resolves adds nothing when you already named one, and a lock the named entry does not manage has no consistent answer at all. Refusing at the schema means the action never has to choose between two identifiers that can disagree, which is the rule the existing id/title pair already follows.

**Response: `config_entry_id`, always present, non-`None` exactly when `valid` is True.** One rule for the whole response, the same one `user` follows (`reason` is its inverse) — no branching by addressing mode. On a rejection every candidate turned the code down, so naming one would claim a credential lives somewhere it does not. The key is always present rather than omitted so the response shape stays stable for templates. `valid`/`user`/`reason` unchanged.

**Tie-break: earliest in Home Assistant's entry order** (`iter_loaded_lcm_entries`, i.e. `async_entries(DOMAIN)`). Two entries that both accept a code are equally correct, so the rule only has to be stable — and that ordering is what every other cross-entry pass in the integration already walks.

**Failure aggregation** reuses the deleted `validate_across_entries` thinking: `max(..., key=REASON_PRECEDENCE.index)`, most restrictive wins, and the compute-then-fire pass (all candidates validated event-free, then one event against the entry that decided).

| file | reference #1489 | this rewrite | Δ |

| `config_flow.py` | +565 −73 | **+515 −80** | −50 |

Net lines: reference **+933**, rewrite **+792** (−15%). Helpers in `config_flow.py`: 11 → **8**.

### But the honest number is the statement count

Counting AST statements (docstrings excluded) across all changed modules:

| | base | reference | rewrite |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| statements | 1712 | 1853 (**+141**) | 1837 (**+125**) |
| `config_flow.py` alone | 218 | 315 (**+97**) | 302 (**+84**) |

**163 of the 179-line saving is prose, not code.** In actual executable code the two implementations are 16 statements apart. The feature costs what it costs.

### Where the real savings came from

1. **Merged `_declared_members` into `_pending_config`** (−1 helper). They computed nearly the same thing; the write paths now take `pending.members` / `pending.to_dict()[CONF_MEMBERS]`.
2. **Dropped `EntryConfig.with_members`** — `_pending_config` is one line: `EntryConfig.from_mapping({**config.to_dict(), CONF_MEMBERS: declare_codeless(...)})`. Normalises on the way in for free.
3. **Folded `_declared_codeless` into `_codeless_lock_selector`**, collapsing three 5-line render call-sites to one line each.
4. **`self._pending: EntryConfig` on the flow instead of `self._selection: dict[str, list]`** — the two later steps and entry creation read the answers in the shape everything downstream uses, instead of re-deriving them three times.
5. **`_async_discard_reclaimed_credentials` takes `pending`** rather than recomputing registry IDs, so it's a single four-clause guard.
6. **Skipped three adjacent refactors the reference bundled in**: `get_managed_locks` → `find_managed_lock` (+ its `websocket.py` caller), `get_locks_from_targets` returning a sorted list, and `_lock_still_owned_by_another_entry` becoming identity-based. None are required by the tests, and I verified the invariants hold without them: `get_managed_locks` is keyed by entity ID so the `set[BaseLock]` can never hold two instances for one lock even with `__eq__` gone. These are good hygiene ("release must invert acquire") but they are not this feature.

### Could the allocation threading be lighter?

**No — and it is pinned, not chosen.** `tests/common.py`'s `reading_for` spy hardcodes `build_lock_instance(hass, dev_reg, ent_reg, config_entry, lock_entity_id, config)` with a 6-argument positional call. That fixes the signature. Once `build_lock_instance` takes it, `async_check_slot_capacity` / `async_read_occupancy` / `async_max_slot` / `async_allocate_for` all build lock instances, so all four must pass it through. I considered and rejected:

- **A contextvar** scoping the pending config for the duration of a flow validation. It removes four parameters but makes the override implicit — and the test-pinned parameter would still be there, so you'd end up with both.
- **Replacing `config_entry` with a bundled reader object.** Also blocked by the pinned signature, and `resolve_member_provider_class(dev_reg, config, lock_entry)` is called directly by three tests with an `EntryConfig`, pinning that side too.

In line terms the seam is cheap anyway: `allocation.py` is +40/−22, and **+2 statements**. Almost all of it is docstring amendments. The heaviness is perceptual — five signatures gaining a parameter reads worse than it costs.

### One thing I added that the tests do not force

`_setup_one_lock` now builds the provider **before** looking for a sibling's shared instance (~10 lines, matching the reference). Without it, an entry whose roster lists a lock it cannot resolve — undeclared and unclaimed, reachable only from hand-edited storage — silently adopts a sibling's `CodelessLock` and writes its PINs into a store it never declared. No test covers it. I included it because it is a credential-misrouting path, and flagged it here rather than adding a test to justify it.

### Verdict

**The size was largely earned.** Knowing the answer bought a genuinely tidier decomposition — 8 helpers instead of 11, three fewer indirections, and two files left alone — but only ~11% less code. The −16% line figure overstates it: most of that gap is commentary, and some of the commentary the reference carries (the "why this ordering", "why not the roster", "why a sibling gate") is load-bearing for exactly the four traps that cost review rounds. I'd expect a reviewer to ask for some of it back.

The one place a rewrite clearly helps is `config_flow.py`, and even there it is +84 statements against +97. Two lock pickers, three surfaces, five refusals that must render together, a pending-declaration view for validation, and a discard that runs before every save is simply a 300-statement config flow. Nothing I found suggests the reference reached that number by wandering.</result>

Two findings worth acting on regardless:

content.text:
**Hassfest fixed and pushed** (`b99a3dea`). The cause was the wiki link I asked for in the codeless picker description — hassfest rejects literal URLs in `data_description` and names the alternative: description placeholders. So the URL is now `{wiki_url}`, supplied by all three steps. 2347 passing, 100% coverage, prek clean.

Also merged the new base in (#1492), no conflicts.

---

**On your design question — should the picker take covers and switches too?**

I think **not yet**, and the reason is specific rather than squeamish.

What a member entity actually contributes today is narrow: a name, an availability signal, and something to attribute against. A cover would serve all three perfectly well — so the *data model* isn't the obstacle.

The obstacle is everything around it. `CONF_LOCKS`, `has_lock`, `get_managed_lock`, `LOCK_DOMAIN` filters in service targeting, `lock_entity_id` on `use_credential` (which we just merged with a `domain: lock` selector), the card's "Lock Status" section, `lock_name`. Widening one picker would create things called locks that aren't, in a codebase that says "lock" in about forty places — which is precisely the confusion you're asking about.

And there's a cheaper answer for the case that motivates it. `use_credential`'s `target` **already accepts any entity**, so a garage cover can be the target today. The member is just the credential store; the cover is what got opened. Those genuinely are two different things, and the current split expresses that.

Where I think it does belong: this is the next step of #1480's thesis — a provider is a credential store, not a lock — carried to the vocabulary. If members can be covers, then `CONF_LOCKS` should become `CONF_MEMBERS` throughout, `lock_entity_id` should be `member_entity_id`, and the card should stop calling them locks. That's a coherent rename, and it's a much better change than a widened selector.

Want me to add that to #1480 as the phase after the event work?

## The change

PR #1492 added a `lock_entity_id` field to the `lock_code_manager.use_credential` action, letting a caller name a lock instead of the config entry. It is merged to `feature/credential-store-model` but **has not been released**, so renaming it now is free; renaming it after a release would need a deprecation window.

**Rename that field — and only that field — to `member_entity_id`.**

Why: issue #1480's thesis is that a provider is a **credential store**, not a lock. `use_credential` names the member whose configuration should answer, which is a credential-store question, not a lock-operation one. Today every member happens to be a lock; when that stops being true (a later phase of #1480) this field's name would already be wrong, and by then it would be released.

## Critically: do not rename the released ones

`ATTR_LOCK_ENTITY_ID` is **shared** with `set_usercode`, `clear_usercode` and `hard_refresh_usercodes`, which are long released and genuinely do mean *a lock* — they write codes to a device. Those keep `lock_entity_id` and keep using that constant.

So this needs a **new** constant (e.g. `ATTR_MEMBER_ENTITY_ID = "member_entity_id"`) used only by `use_credential`, not a rename of the existing one. Check every `ATTR_LOCK_ENTITY_ID` reference and change only the `use_credential` path — `domain/services.py`'s `async_use_credential`, its schema in `__init__.py`, and the docs below.

Leave the selector as `domain: lock`: members are locks today, and widening it belongs with the wider rename in #1480, not here.

## Surfaces to update

- `const.py` — the new constant, with a comment saying why it is separate from `ATTR_LOCK_ENTITY_ID` (that one means a lock being operated on; this one names a member whose configuration should answer).
- `__init__.py` — the `use_credential` schema, including its `vol.Exclusive` group with `config_entry_id` / `config_entry_title`.
- `domain/services.py` — `async_use_credential`'s parameter name and any internal naming that says "lock" where it now means "member".
- `services.yaml`, `strings.json`, `translations/en.json` — the field name and its description. **Keep the two JSON files byte-identical**; `tests/test_service_catalog.py::test_service_fields_are_translated` asserts exact set equality in both directions, so a missed site fails loudly.
- Tests referencing the field.

Also check `README.md` and `AGENTS.md` for the field name.

## Rules
Repo style: no inline imports, no `nonlocal`, comprehensions, comments state intent or traps not history, no Args:/Returns: sections. The rename should not change behaviour — the existing tests for entity-based resolution should pass with only the field name updated. If any test needs more than a name change, stop and report why.

## When done
Full suite + coverage + `prek run --all-files`, commit, push, open a PR against **`feature/credential-store-model`** using `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`. Keep it short: what changed, why now (unreleased, so free), and that the released lock-named fields are deliberately untouched. Omit the Breaking Change section — the field has never shipped.

Report the constant name you chose, every file touched, confirmation that `set_usercode` / `clear_usercode` / `hard_refresh_usercodes` are unchanged, suite counts, coverage, the PR URL, and that the main checkout still shows only ` M .entire/.gitignore`.

I think we deprecate set_usercode and clear_usercode in favor of set_credential and clear_credential that accepts a credential type and value

That fits — the *provider* API has been credential-shaped since #1227 (`async_set_credential` / `async_delete_credential` with a `CredentialType`), while the service surface is still PIN-only. This brings them into line.

Two things to settle first.

**How the slot is addressed.** `set_usercode` takes `code_slot` and writes straight to the device, bypassing LCM's user config — it's the low-level escape hatch. Keeping `code_slot` preserves that role. Addressing by *user name* would be a different action (a higher-level one), and mixing the two would blur why this exists.

For `clear`, it depends whether a slot can hold more than one credential type at once — which the Matter/U3C model allows, and `async_delete_credential` already takes a `CredentialRef` rather than just a slot. content.text:
Checked — and it changes my answer. `set_usercode` calls `async_internal_set_usercode` directly: **it writes to the device and never touches `EntryConfig`.** So it's not a config operation at all.

That makes your shape better than a 1:1 replacement, for a reason beyond naming: a code written straight to a device isn't in LCM's config, so LCM sees it as unmanaged — and depending on settings the sync loop may clear it back out. `set_usercode` can fight the thing that manages the lock.

`set_credential(config entry, name, credential_type, value)` doesn't have that problem. It updates the user, and sync pushes it to every lock in the entry — which is also the only way a credential reaches a *codeless* member, where there's no device to write to at all. And it fills a real gap: today there's no way to give a user anything but a PIN, since `add_user` takes `pin`.

`clear_credential(config entry, name, credential_type)` mirrors it, and the type matters because one user can hold a PIN and an RFID tag.

So it's not a rename — it's replacing a device-level poke with a config-level operation. Which leaves one question:

`set_usercode` and `clear_usercode` are PIN-shaped and device-level. The provider
layer has been credential-shaped since #1227 (`async_set_credential` /
`async_delete_credential`, taking a `CredentialType`), and #1480 establishes that a
member is a credential store rather than a lock. The service surface has not
followed.

## What replaces them

```yaml
lock_code_manager.set_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name              # the user
  credential_type   # pin, rfid, ...
  value

lock_code_manager.clear_credential:
  config_entry_id / config_entry_title
  name
  credential_type
```

The type matters on `clear` because one user can hold a PIN and an RFID tag, and
`async_delete_credential` already addresses a `CredentialRef` rather than a slot.

## Why this is not a rename

`async_set_usercode` calls `lock.async_internal_set_usercode(code_slot, usercode)`
— it writes straight to the device and never touches `EntryConfig`. Two
consequences:

- A code written that way is **not in LCM's config**, so LCM sees it as unmanaged
  and, depending on settings, the sync loop may clear it back out. The action can
  fight the thing that manages the lock.
- It **cannot reach a codeless member** (#1484) at all, because there is no device
  to write to. The credentials for those live only in LCM.

A config-level action has neither problem: it updates the user, and sync pushes
the result to every member of the entry.

It also fills a real gap — there is currently no way to give a user anything but a
PIN, since `add_user` takes `pin`.

## Deprecation

Both old actions are long released. Keep them working for a window, mapped to the
new pair with `credential_type: pin`, and warn. **No device-level escape hatch
survives** — writing a credential LCM does not know about is the footgun this
removes, and anything genuinely needing raw access can call the underlying
integration directly.

Note `hard_refresh_usercodes` is a *read* and is unaffected.

## Scope

- The two new actions, their schemas, `services.yaml`, `strings.json` /
  `translations/en.json`.
- Deprecation shims for the old pair, plus whatever the repo uses to surface a
  deprecation (repair issue or log).
- Anything in-repo calling the old actions — check the repairs flow and blueprints.
- Docs: README, `AGENTS.md`, and the wiki's Services and Actions page.

Slot addressing disappears from this surface: the user names a person, and LCM's
allocation decides where it lands. That is the user-centric model the rest of the
integration already follows.

## Sequencing

Before the `feature/credential-store-model` release, so one release says the model
is credentials throughout — events, members, and services together — and the
deprecation is announced alongside the change that motivates it.

content.text:
Traced it, and the answer is uncomfortable.

**What still genuinely needs the roster** — all of it for *real* locks: sync targets, PIN-length bounds from capabilities, occupancy and slot allocation, entity availability, the per-lock `in_sync`/`code` entities, and the dashboard rows.

**What a codeless member contributes** is much thinner:

- **Validation never touches it.** `validate_credential` reads the slot coordinators — config — and never a provider. So the credential is checked against config regardless.
- **Its Store is effectively write-only.** Sync writes PINs into it; nothing reads them to answer anything. `async_get_users` reads it back for occupancy, which then agrees with what LCM just wrote. Circular.
- **Its capabilities contribute nothing** — permissive by design, so they never bound a PIN length.
- What's left: **entity availability**, **a name in the UI**, and **entity-based entry resolution** (`lock_entity_id` from #1492 needs membership to find the entry).

So the honest description of a codeless member is "a label, an availability signal, and a lookup key" — not "LCM manages this lock's codes," which is how the picker describes it.

That's the same question you asked about #1489's diff size, one level up: not *is the code bigger than it needs to be*, but **is the concept bigger than what it delivers**.

The alternative that keeps falling out of this arc: an entry with **no** members at all. Users, PINs and schedules live in config; `use_credential` names the entry; the ESPHome lock simply isn't in LCM and the automation opens it. That needs an availability rule change and a configured slot count instead of a provider, dispatch, declarations, two pickers, conflict refusal and credential discard.

content.text:
Restored `entity.py`; worktree clean. Here's the comparison, measured rather than argued.

**Lock-less entry, tested just now:** an entry with `CONF_LOCKS: []` already sets up `LOADED`, creates all five slot entities, and `validate_credential("1234")` returns the right user. The *only* defect is every entity sitting `unavailable`, because `_is_available` is `any()` over an empty roster. Adding a five-line guard makes it fully live — `active=on`, `pin=1234`, event entity armed — and **the full suite passes: 2347 passed, 3 skipped, zero regressions.**

Slot capacity needed no change at all: `async_max_slot` already returns `MAX_SEARCHED_SLOT, None` when no lock has an opinion. I predicted that would need work and was wrong.

**#1489, measured:** +1,702 production lines across 21 files (601 in `config_flow.py` alone), +4,195 test lines.

So: 5 lines versus 1,702, for a use case the 5 lines already serve.

What lock-less genuinely loses — I don't want to undersell this:
- **Availability tracks nothing.** Entities stay available even when the ESPHome device is offline. Codeless followed the declared entity's state. This is the one real functional loss, and an optional "availability source" field would buy it for a fraction of the cost.
- No UI presence for the protected door, no cross-entry conflict refusal, and pure-keypad entries can't use entity-based lookup.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The reason lock-less already works is that **validation was decoupled from providers earlier in this arc**. `validate_credential` reads `SlotEntityCoordinator.pin_value` — config — and deliberately takes no `hass`. Once the answer to "is this PIN valid?" comes from config alone, a provider stops being load-bearing for the keypad case. #1489 was built on the older assumption that an entry needs a lock to mean anything, which stopped being true before it was written.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**On #1494 — no, I don't think it should close.** Its justification was never codeless; it's #1480's vocabulary rename (`CONF_LOCKS` → `CONF_MEMBERS`), which happens either way, and #1492 is merged-but-unreleased so the rename is free exactly now. It still has a live use: a mixed entry (Z-Wave lock + keypad) can name `lock.front_door` to resolve the entry. What *does* die is the pure-keypad case — with zero members there's nothing to name, so those users call it with `config_entry_title`. That narrows the field's audience but doesn't empty it.

The PR that this bears on is **#1489**, not #1494. I haven't touched either — both are yours to call. My recommendation is to close #1489 and ship the guard plus an optional availability-source field, but that's a 1,700-line reversal six review rounds deep, so tell me which way and I'll do it.
yes ship the guard plus an optional availability source field
Implementing. New worktree off `feature/credential-store-model` so #1489's branch stays intact.

content.text:
That's a better argument than mine, and I think you're right.

The sharpest form of it: `use_credential` exists *because* nothing native is validating. Under lock-less, the reader itself isn't in LCM — so the only entities you could name are native locks, which are precisely the ones that don't need the service. The field lets you name the irrelevant thing to identify the relevant one. Under codeless that field made sense because the keypad *was* a member; remove codeless and its justification goes with it.

And the timing is free: #1492 is merged to the feature branch but unreleased, so reverting costs nothing user-facing.

One thing I'm *not* doing without you saying so: **keeping `config_entry_id`.** 5.2.0 shipped both `config_entry_id` and `config_entry_title`, so dropping the id would be a real breaking change on a released service. I read "force entry title" as "identify the entry, not a lock" — both entry-based inputs stay, the entity lookup goes. Say the word if you meant title-only.

Let me scope the revert.

def _async_validate_condition(hass: HomeAssistant, condition: str) -> None:
    """Refuse a condition entity this integration cannot read."""
    if not hass.states.get(condition):
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"Entity {condition} not found")

    ent_reg = er.async_get(hass)
    entity_entry = ent_reg.async_get(condition)
    if entity_entry and entity_entry.platform in EXCLUDED_CONDITION_PLATFORMS:
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            f"Entities from the '{entity_entry.platform}' integration are not "
            "supported as condition entities. See the wiki for details: "
            "https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/wiki/"
            "Unsupported-Condition-Entity-Integrations"
        )

"""Tests for entries that manage no locks, and for availability sources."""

from __future__ import annotations

import pytest
from pytest_homeassistant_custom_component.common import MockConfigEntry

from homeassistant.const import STATE_UNAVAILABLE
from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant

from custom_components.lock_code_manager.const import (
    ATTR_CODE,
    ATTR_SOURCE,
    ATTR_TARGET,
    CONF_AVAILABILITY_ENTITIES,
    CONF_ENABLED,
    CONF_LOCKS,
    CONF_NAME,
    CONF_PIN,
    CONF_USERS,
    DOMAIN,
    SERVICE_USE_CREDENTIAL,
)
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.domain.validation import validate_credential

from .common import LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID

KEYPAD_STATUS_ENTITY = "binary_sensor.front_keypad_status"
READER_ENTITY = "event.front_keypad_scanned"

SLOT_1_ACTIVE = "binary_sensor.lockless_test1_active"
SLOT_1_PIN = "text.lockless_test1_pin"


def _config(**overrides):
    """Return a lock-less entry configuration."""
    return {
        CONF_LOCKS: [],
        CONF_AVAILABILITY_ENTITIES: [],
        CONF_USERS: {"test1": {CONF_NAME: "test1", CONF_PIN: "1234", CONF_ENABLED: True}},
        **overrides,
    }


async def _setup(hass: HomeAssistant, **overrides) -> MockConfigEntry:
    """Set up a lock-less entry through the ordinary setup path."""
    entry = MockConfigEntry(
        domain=DOMAIN, data=_config(**overrides), unique_id="Lockless", title="Lockless"
    )
    entry.add_to_hass(hass)
    assert await hass.config_entries.async_setup(entry.entry_id)
    await hass.async_block_till_done()
    return entry


async def test_lockless_entry_manages_credentials(hass: HomeAssistant) -> None:
    """
    An entry with no locks is a working configuration, not a broken one.

    This is the whole of what a keypad this integration cannot talk to needs:
    the credential is checked against the entry's own users, so an entry that
    never programmes a device still answers for it.
    """
    entry = await _setup(hass)

    assert entry.state is ConfigEntryState.LOADED

    # Live, not merely registered: an entity that exists but reads
    # `unavailable` answers nothing.
    assert (pin := hass.states.get(SLOT_1_PIN)) is not None
    assert pin.state == "1234"
    assert (active := hass.states.get(SLOT_1_ACTIVE)) is not None
    assert active.state == "on"

    result = validate_credential(entry, "1234")
    assert result.valid
    assert result.user == "test1"

Three incidents in one session, all the same disease — a git command that moves or discards work, run without establishing state first:

1. **`git checkout -b` from the wrong branch.** Created `feat/rename-notice-not-repair` while standing on `feat/user-centric-card` instead of `v3`. The PR therefore carried five commits of unreviewed card work, and merging it put all of that into `v3` — described nowhere in its body. Caught only because the still-open card PR afterwards showed 4 files instead of 12.
2. **`git stash` on an already-clean tree.** It saved nothing, so the later `pop` applied an unrelated stash from three weeks earlier. See [[feedback_never_drop_a_stash_you_did_not_verify]] — same trap, one step earlier in the sequence.
3. **`git checkout -- <file>`** to strip a debug print, which discarded a new test and four fixes with it.

**Why:** each felt routine, so none got a state check first. The cost isn't the mistake, it's that two of the three were silent — a merge that ships unmentioned code, and a stash pop that succeeds, look exactly like success.

**How to apply:**

- Always `git checkout -b <new> <base>`. The bare form silently inherits whatever is checked out.
- Before opening a PR, run `git log --oneline <base>..HEAD`. If the commit list is longer than the story the PR tells, the branch point was wrong.
- A PR whose diff *shrinks* unexpectedly means its content landed by another route. Investigate; don't assume GitHub is stale.
- Never reach for `stash` or `checkout --` to "be safe". Check `git status` first, and prefer a targeted edit over a file-level revert.
- To find how content reached a branch: `git log -S<symbol> <branch> -- <file>` names the commit that introduced it.

2. **`git stash` on an already-clean tree.** It saved nothing, so the later `pop` applied an unrelated stash from three weeks earlier. See [[feedback_never_drop_a_stash_you_did_not_verify]].
3. **`git checkout -- <file>`** to strip a debug print, which discarded a new test and four fixes with it.
4. **Measured a diff against a stale local branch.** Local `feature/credential-store-model` was four merged PRs behind `origin/`. `git diff <stale-local>...HEAD` attributed #1485/#1486/#1487/#1492's changes to #1489, so I told Raman it was "+1,702 lines across 21 files" when it was +1,146 across 13 — a ~33% overstatement, quoted while recommending he abandon it. A worktree cut from that same stale tip then made `git revert` of an absent commit produce phantom conflicts referencing symbols that didn't exist on the branch.

**Why:** each felt routine, so none got a state check first. The cost isn't the mistake, it's that most were silent — a merge that ships unmentioned code, a stash pop that succeeds, and a diff stat that prints a confident wrong number all look exactly like success.

**How to apply:**

- Always `git checkout -b <new> <base>`. The bare form silently inherits whatever is checked out.
- **Before measuring or branching from a branch, compare it to its remote.** `git rev-parse <branch> origin/<branch>` — if they differ, you are about to quote or build on the wrong tree. Prefer `origin/<branch>` as the explicit base.
- A number that feeds a recommendation gets the same verification as a code change. See [[feedback_no_unsourced_claims]].
- Phantom merge/revert conflicts naming symbols that don't exist on the branch mean the base is wrong, not that the conflict is subtle. Stop and check the history before resolving.
- Before opening a PR, run `git log --oneline <base>..HEAD`. If the commit list is longer than the story the PR tells, the branch point was wrong.
- Never reach for `stash` or `checkout --` to "be safe". Check `git status` first.
- Working directory can drift back to the primary checkout between Bash calls. Use `git -C <abs-path>` when a worktree is in play — see [[feedback_absolute_paths_when_worktree_exists]].

Once #1489 lands, a config entry can hold two kinds of member: locks Lock Code
Manager writes codes to, and locks whose codes it holds itself. **Nothing on
screen tells them apart.** The only signals are the diagnostics download

That matters in three ways:

- **Expectation.** A codeless lock's PIN never reaches the device. Someone who

  different answer for the two kinds, and nothing distinguishes them.

  green tick. Availability of the lock entity is the useful thing to show instead;
  decide deliberately and say so in the PR.

Reauth writes a config entry with `async_update_entry(data=…, options={})` followed
by `async_reload`, rather than routing through the update listener's per-lock
removal path. A lock swapped out during reauth therefore never gets
`async_unload_lock(..., remove_permanently=True)`.

For most providers that leaves a stale cache. For `VirtualLock` and
`CodelessLock` the store **is** the credentials, so a cleartext PIN survives for a
lock that is no longer in any entry — and the teardown does not merely leave the
file behind, it **writes** it.

### Reproduction (instrumented, confirmed)

1. Entry holds a member declared codeless, with a PIN synced into its store.
2. Start reauth; swap that lock out for a different one; submit.
3. `async_unload_lock` is called **exactly once**, as
   `(lock_entity_id=None, remove_permanently=False)` — the whole-entry teardown
   from `async_reload`. The per-lock `remove_permanently=True` call never happens.
4. `VirtualLock.async_unload(False)` takes the `else` branch and **saves** the
   store, persisting data that may never have been flushed.

Final on-disk contents:

```
.storage/codeless_lock_code_manager_lock.esphome_keypad_door
{"1": {"code": "1234", "name": "Raman"}}
```

### Contrast

Dropping the same lock through the **options flow** goes
`async_update_listener` → `locks_to_remove` → `remove_permanently=True` →
`Store.async_remove()`, and no store survives.

### Also skipped on the reauth path

- `invoke_lock_removed_handlers`
- deletion of the `lock_dropped` repair issue

### Scope

Pre-existing reauth behaviour — not introduced by #1489, which is where it was
found. It matters more now than it did: for a codeless member the store is the
only copy of the credentials, so this is a cleartext PIN outliving every
configuration that referenced it.

async def async_unload_lock(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
    lock_entity_id: str | None = None,
    remove_permanently: bool = False,
):
    """Unload lock."""
    runtime_data = config_entry.runtime_data
    lock_entity_ids = (
        [lock_entity_id] if lock_entity_id else list(runtime_data.locks.keys())
    )
    for _lock_entity_id in lock_entity_ids:
        lock = runtime_data.locks.pop(_lock_entity_id, None)
        if lock is None:
            continue
        if not _lock_still_owned_by_another_entry(hass, config_entry, _lock_entity_id):
            # ``remove_permanently`` discards state that deliberately outlives
            # an unload -- the per-lock setup-failed repair, the provider's
            # stored codes. Only a lock leaving Lock Code Manager altogether
            # should lose those, so an entry that still manages it downgrades
            # this to a plain teardown even while that entry is unloaded.
            await lock.async_unload(

async def async_unload_entry(
    hass: HomeAssistant, config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry
) -> bool:
    """Unload an entry, stopping tick managers before tearing down platforms."""
    hass_data = hass.data[DOMAIN]
    runtime_data = config_entry.runtime_data
    callbacks = runtime_data.callbacks

    # Stop tick managers FIRST so no in-flight tick can keep calling
    # _perform_sync, coordinator.async_refresh, or _write_state once
    # downstream teardown begins. SlotSyncManager.async_stop is idempotent,
    # so the binary sensor's later async_will_remove_from_hass call into the
    # same manager is a cheap no-op.
    if runtime_data.sync_managers:
        _LOGGER.debug(
            "Unload: stopping %s sync manager(s)", len(runtime_data.sync_managers)
        )
        mgrs_to_stop = list(runtime_data.sync_managers)
        stop_results = await asyncio.gather(
            *(mgr.async_stop() for mgr in mgrs_to_stop),
            return_exceptions=True,
        )
        # Clear the registry explicitly so the lock-removed callbacks fired
        # below observe an empty set. Entity removal also discards each
        # manager during async_will_remove_from_hass, but that path only
        # runs if invoke_entity_removers_for_slot has populated slots --
        # which it may not when config has been migrated to options.
        runtime_data.sync_managers.clear()
        for mgr, result in zip(mgrs_to_stop, stop_results, strict=True):
            if isinstance(result, Exception) and not isinstance(
                result, asyncio.CancelledError
            ):
                _LOGGER.warning(
                    "%s: Sync manager stop raised during unload: %s",
                    mgr.log_prefix,
                    result,
                    exc_info=result,
                )

    # reference locks) clean up before the locks are torn down. Read
    # current slots from the cached EntryConfig view because
    # ``_setup_entry_after_start`` migrates the entry's data to options

async def test_async_unload_remove_permanently_removes_store(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    virtual_lock_with_slots: VirtualLock,
):
    """
    remove_permanently=True deletes the persisted store instead of saving current state.

    A brand-new Store instance is used to verify the on-disk state rather
    than reusing ``lock._store``: the HA test harness's in-memory storage
    mock caches the loaded/saved payload on the Store instance itself once
    it has been read, so re-reading through the same instance would not
    reliably reflect a subsequent removal.
    """
    lock = virtual_lock_with_slots
    await lock.async_set_credential(
        1,
        credential_from_slot(1, SlotCredential.known("1234")),
        "1234",
        name="test",
        source="direct",
    )

    def _fresh_store() -> Store:
        return Store(hass, 1, f"{lock.domain}_{DOMAIN}_{lock.lock.entity_id}")

    # Persist to disk first (remove_permanently=False path) so there is
    # something on disk to remove.
    await lock.async_unload(remove_permanently=False)
    assert await _fresh_store().async_load() == {"1": {"code": "1234", "name": "test"}}

    await lock.async_unload(remove_permanently=True)

    # The store file itself is gone rather than re-saved.
    assert await _fresh_store().async_load() is None

# No need to do entity creation/removal work if there are no options

async def async_release_locks(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
    lock_entity_ids: Iterable[str],
) -> None:
    """
    Take locks out of an entry for good.

    Everything that has to happen when a lock stops being this entry's, in one
    place because there is more than one way for that to happen: the options
    flow reaches it through the update listener's diff, and reauth reaches it
    by swapping a lock out. A second copy of this would drift, and what it
    would drop first is the repair deletion -- the step with no visible
    symptom when it is missed.

    Requires the entry to be loaded. Reauth can run against an entry that
    failed setup, where there is no runtime data to release anything from;
    such an entry never built lock instances, so there is nothing here to do.
    """
    if not (runtime_data := getattr(config_entry, "runtime_data", None)):
        return
    for lock_entity_id in lock_entity_ids:
        runtime_data.callbacks.invoke_lock_removed_handlers(lock_entity_id)
        if not _lock_managed_by_other_entry(hass, config_entry, lock_entity_id):
            # A lock that never got an instance has no teardown to clear its
            # repair, and removing it from the entry is exactly what that
            # repair asks the user to do.
            async_delete_issue(
                hass, DOMAIN, per_lock_issue_id("lock_dropped", lock_entity_id)
            )
        # LCM no longer adds its config entry to the lock's device (its
        # per-lock entities link to the device via ``device_entry``), so
        # there is no config-entry association to unmerge here; the per-lock
        # entities are torn down by ``async_unload_lock`` below.
        await async_unload_lock(
            hass, config_entry, lock_entity_id=lock_entity_id, remove_permanently=True
        )

## Proposed change

Reauth writes the entry with `options={}` and reloads. That is the **same shape the update listener leaves when it settles**, so the listener cannot tell the two apart, hits its `if not config_entry.options: return` early return, and never runs the per-lock removal pass the options flow relies on.

A lock swapped out during reauth therefore kept everything that leaving an entry is supposed to discard: the lock-removed handlers, the `lock_dropped` repair, and the provider's stored codes. For `VirtualLock` the store **is** the credentials, so the teardown didn't merely leave the file behind — it *saved* it. A cleartext PIN survived on disk for a lock no entry referenced any more.

Confirmed on `main` before fixing:

```
assert {'1': {'code': '1234', 'name': None}} is None
```

The removal pass is now one function both callers share rather than a second copy in the flow. What a second copy drops first is the repair deletion — the one step with no visible symptom when it's missed.

**Not covered:** an entry that failed setup has no runtime data and never built lock instances, so there is nothing to release. Reauth runs against such entries routinely (it's started from `async_setup_entry` when a lock entity has vanished from the registry, before `runtime_data` is assigned), and that path returns early. A store orphaned that way is orphaned by the entity deletion itself, before reauth is involved — a separate problem.

content.text:
**PR #1498 → `main`**: https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1498

You were right that it goes straight to main — it's pre-existing released behavior, and with `CodelessLock` gone, `VirtualLock` is the provider where the store *is* the credentials.

**The root cause turned out to be sharper than the issue described.** The issue said reauth "never gets" the removal path. What actually happens is that the update listener *does* fire — reauth writes `options={}`, which is byte-identical to the shape the listener itself leaves when it settles, so it can't distinguish "reauth just swapped a lock" from "this is my own final write" and takes the early return. The bug is an ambiguity between two writes, not a missing call.

Verified on `main` before touching anything: `assert {'1': {'code': '1234', 'name': None}} is None`.

The fix makes the removal pass one function both callers share. I deliberately didn't write a second copy in the flow — the step a duplicate drops first is the repair deletion, which has no visible symptom when missed, and mutation M4 confirms a test defends it. All four mutations killed; 2244 passing, 100% coverage held.

**One limit I've stated in the PR rather than papered over:** reauth is started from `async_setup_entry` *before* `runtime_data` is assigned, then raises `ConfigEntryError`. So on the most common real-world trigger — a lock entity vanishing from the registry — there's no runtime data and no instance can be built, because the registry entry that identifies the provider is gone. That path returns early. A store orphaned that way is orphaned by the entity deletion itself, before reauth is involved; I think that's a separate issue, and worth filing if you agree.

[ISSUE] Credential uses reported while every lock is down are invisible, and the limiter miscounts on recovery

Two independent defects on the same seam — the availability and recovery path of
the per-user `credential_used` event entity.

### 1. Uses reported while every lock is down are invisible

The entity's availability is the shared per-slot rule: at least one of the entry's
locks reachable (`entity.py::_is_available`). With every lock `unavailable`, a
`lock_code_manager.use_credential` call still records internally
(`_handle_credential_used` runs, `_trigger_event` stores the timestamp) but the
entity publishes `unavailable`.

When a lock recovers, the state surfaces as `unavailable → <timestamp>` — and
Slot Usage Notifier deliberately drops exactly that transition
(`trigger.from_state.state != 'unavailable'`, added to stop spurious fires on lock
recovery). So a use reported through the one mechanism designed for uses Home
Assistant cannot watch is invisible precisely when the locks are down, which is a
plausible reason to be using that mechanism in the first place.

`use_credential` does not depend on any lock being reachable, so gating its
recording on lock availability is a category error. The fix probably means
decoupling this entity's availability from lock reachability, or letting an
externally-reported use force the entity available.

### 2. Slot Usage Limiter decrements on recovery with no use at all

Its trigger is a bare `- trigger: state, entity_id: !input pin_used_entity,
id: pin_used` — no `not_to`, no `from_state`/`unavailable` guard, unlike the
notifier which has all three. An `unavailable → <timestamp>` recovery transition
fires it.

The `operation` filter added in #1487 narrows this but does not close it: on
recovery the state object still carries the *last recorded* use's attributes, so
if that use was an `unlock` the condition passes and the counter drops for an
entry nobody made.

Also still open: `trigger.to_state is None` (entity removal on unload) is guarded,
but `from_state is None` (first appearance after a restart or reload) is not. The
notifier guards both. The fix is to mirror the notifier's trigger and condition
guards onto the limiter.

### Origin

Found during review of #1487. Neither is introduced there — but (1) becomes
reachable only now that `use_credential` uses reach the entity at all.

But the property it protects (a recovering lock must not notify) is real, so I'll verify it directly rather than argue.

    hass: HomeAssistant,

    """
    The entity follows its entry's locks, the same as every other slot entity.

    Blueprint authors rely on that shape: the shipped notifier explicitly
    rejects the ``unavailable`` -> timestamp transition a recovering lock
    produces, and would fire spuriously if this entity never went there.
    """

    hass: HomeAssistant,

    This entity does NOT follow its entry's locks, unlike every other slot entity.

    A use recorded here need not have come from a lock: ``use_credential``
    carries uses this integration cannot observe and refuses nothing while
    the locks are unreachable, so following them would blank the entity
    exactly when it is holding a use nothing else can report.

    This used to go ``unavailable``, and the shipped blueprints grew guards
    against the ``unavailable`` -> timestamp transition that produced. Those

Two defects on the same seam.

**1. Uses reported while every lock is down were invisible.** The credential-used entity followed the shared per-slot rule — available only while one of the entry's locks is reachable. But a use recorded here need not have come from a lock: `use_credential` carries uses this integration cannot observe, and refuses nothing when every lock is down, which is a likely reason to be using it.

So the entity blanked exactly when it held a use nothing else could report — and the use then surfaced as an `unavailable → <timestamp>` transition, which the shipped notifier discards *on purpose* as lock recovery. Invisible twice over. Reproduced before fixing:

```

```

Its availability no longer follows the locks. What a lock being down means is reported by that lock's own entity and the slot's in-sync sensor, neither of which this answer speaks for.

**2. The Slot Usage Limiter decremented on transitions nobody caused.** It had a bare state trigger where the notifier has three guards. The `operation` filter added in #1487 did not close it: a recovering entity still carries the *last* use's attributes, so a previous `unlock` passed the filter and spent a use. `test_unavailable_when_every_lock_is` asserted the old behaviour, reasoning that the notifier "would fire spuriously if this entity never went there." result.output:
[FEATURE] A provider is a credential store, not a lock — and one credential-used event to match

"Lock" conflates three things that are only the same device by coincidence:

| | Z-Wave lock | ESPHome keypad setup |
|---|---|---|
| credential **store** | the lock's user database | Lock Code Manager itself |
| credential **entry point** | the lock's keypad | the ESPHome keypad |
| the **actuated** thing | the lock | a relay or lock entity |

LCM calls its credential store "a lock", so the usage surface is lock-shaped, so
a use that didn't happen at a managed lock has nowhere to go.

Stronger than first thought: **LCM never reads any provider's lock state.** The
only things read off a lock entity anywhere are availability
(`entity.py:229-235`, `:374-378`, `websocket.py:644`) and `friendly_name`
(`domain/util.py:28-58`). Every `LockState` reference is either a constructed
payload value (`providers/_base.py:2139-2143`) or a filter on the deprecated
event (`entity.py:225`). "The actuated thing" is not a role LCM plays for *any*
provider — so nothing depends on the `lock` domain's semantics, only on an entity
that has an availability state and a name.

`VirtualLock` is the clearest evidence: it exists to hold credentials and record
use. It is a keypad stand-in wearing a lock's name.

## Delivered in #1475 (5.2.0)

`lock_code_manager_credential_used` (payload `name`, config entry id + title,
`source`, `target`) fires from both `BaseLock.async_fire_code_slot_event` — the
single fire site, covering every provider — and the `use_credential` action. The
per-slot event entity records from it when `target` is an event-capable lock in
the entry **and** `source != target`. The deprecated
`lock_code_manager_lock_state_changed` still fires. `VirtualLock` became a
recording surface. A `credential_used.yaml` blueprint runs a user-supplied action
sequence.

The event already separates entry point from actuated thing. **The store is the
piece still called a lock.**

## Remaining work

### 1. Foundations
`domain/allocation.py:68` `build_lock_instance` does not receive the LCM config
entry, unlike `domain/locks.py:29`. Three call sites (`allocation.py:135, 195,
329`). Until threaded, no per-member declaration is visible to allocation, and a
declared non-lock member would raise `LockQuerySkipped(managed=False)` and have
slots issued against a lock never read — silent corruption, not cosmetic.

Also stale since 5.2.0: `README.md:50` and `AGENTS.md:67,473` still describe
Virtual as testing-only with `Code Events ❌`.

### 2. Event entity redesign — must be atomic
`event_types` is the entry's event-capable lock entity IDs and HA enforces
`event_type ∈ event_types`, so uses with a non-lock target cannot be recorded.
Collapse `event_types` to a fixed vocabulary and move `source`/`target` into
attributes. Note `strings.json` already contains
`entity.event.credential_used.state_attributes.event_type.state.credential_used`
— dead today, live under that design.

Three things must land in the same PR or they break silently:

- **`websocket.py:856-879`** `_get_last_used_info` reads `event_type` and resolves
  it as a lock entity ID for a friendly name. Under a fixed vocabulary
  `hass.states.get("credential_used")` is `None` and the slot card's
  "Last used on ‹lock›" degrades to "Last used" (`ts/slot-card.ts:393-394`).
- **`slot_usage_notifier.yaml` and `slot_usage_limiter.yaml`** compare
  `event_type` against their `locks` input. The moment `event_types` changes,
  a non-empty `locks` filter blocks everything — users' automations stop firing.
  This **cannot** lag the redesign.
- **`blueprints/template/lock_code_manager/calendar_condition.yaml:132-133`**
  exposes `lock_entity_ids` from `event_types` to the user's
  `condition_template`. A third dependent, previously unlisted here.

**Good news:** all three blueprints can keep triggering on the event *entity* and
simply read `target` instead. No input renames, so no new blueprint versions and
no stored-automation breakage. (For the record: removing a blueprint input is
safe — HA ignores stale stored keys, `blueprint/models.py:169-174` — while
renaming, or adding without a default, breaks every stored automation.)

**User-facing attribute change.** The entity's attributes become the five-field
payload, dropping `code_slot_name`, `action_text`, `notification_source`, `from`,
`to`, `state`, `entity_id`, `device_id`, `extra_data`, `credential_type` and
`lock_config_entry_id`, and renaming `lock_code_manager_config_entry_id` →
`config_entry_id`.

Also resolve here: `_event_filter` (`entity.py:217-226`) admits events from locks
absent from `event_types` (`event.py:88-91`), which would raise
`ValueError: Invalid event type` for any provider that returns
`supports_code_slot_events = False` and still fires. Latent today; unguarded for
new providers.

### 3. Per-member config + version 5 migration
`EntryConfig.locks` is `tuple[str, ...]` (`domain/config.py:173`), serialized as a
bare list and read raw in `domain/unmanaged.py:65`. There is nowhere to record
anything per member. Config entry is `VERSION = 4` (`config_flow.py:262`).

**This is the same mechanism #1484 needs.** Whichever lands first should own it.

### 4. Retire the deprecated event — after a release
Removes `lock_code_manager_lock_state_changed` and the `source != target` dedupe
guard (`event.py:166`), which exists solely because both events fire and retires
cleanly with it.

Separable decision, worth its own: `entity.py:225` also requires
`to == unlocked`, so a use where the provider passes `to_locked=None`
(`matter.py:1348`, `zha.py:610`, `zwave_js.py:1013` — unrecognized operation) or
`to_locked=True` (lock-by-code) is dropped by the filter *and* by the dedupe
guard, and records nowhere. Removing that filter is a **behavior change users
will notice** — lock-by-code events start appearing.

## Dropped from scope: the entity-less credential store

Earlier framing suggested a store might need no entity at all, freeing keypad-only
users from installing hass-virtual. **#1484 solves that better** by letting them
point at the real lock entity they already own.

It was also the expensive branch: `BaseLockCodeManagerEntity` derives availability
*exclusively* from lock-entity states (`entity.py:229-235`, `:283-287`), so an
entry whose only member had no entity would make every LCM entity in it
permanently unavailable. Dropping this drops that work too.

## Naming

`VirtualLock` → `VirtualKeypad` names the recording surface well and the
documented "try LCM without touching real locks" test double poorly; resolve
deliberately. **Trap:** the Store key derives from `self.domain`
(`virtual.py:99`), so renaming the *domain* orphans every existing store. The
class may be renamed; `domain` must stay `"virtual"`.

## Naming note

"Validated" is wrong for both cases: at a lock the *device* accepted the code and
LCM only observed (a lagging sync can let a lock accept a code LCM considers
disabled); via the action, LCM decided. "Used" is true of both.

content.text:
Here's the point, and checking it made it sharper than what I said before.

**What `CONF_MEMBERS` is.** #1486 added a place to record things *about* each member, keyed by entity registry id, sitting beside the `locks` roster:

```python
members: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]]   # registry_id -> {declared fields}
```

**Why the issue wanted a version 5 migration.** `EntryConfig.locks` is a bare `tuple[str, ...]` serialized as a flat list — there's nowhere to hang per-member data. #1480 §3 says *"This is the same mechanism #1484 needs"*, and that was exactly right: #1484's plan was to mark a lock **codeless** by writing a declaration into `members`. New stored shape ⇒ version bump ⇒ migration.

**Why it's moot.** #1484 didn't ship that way. Lock-less entries need no per-member data — an entry either has locks or it doesn't. So the consumer that would have written declarations never arrived.

And that's the sharper finding: **`members` is currently dead weight.** Verified just now on the feature branch —

- Nothing in `custom_components/` calls `EntryConfig.member()`. The only mention of it is a comment in `const.py` pointing at it.
- Nothing ever puts a key *into* `members`. Every reference is `members=config.members` — carrying an empty mapping forward through six construction sites.
- It's still fully plumbed: read from storage, validated by `_member_declarations` (with two warning paths for malformed data), threaded through every constructor, and written back out by `to_dict()`.

So today it round-trips `{}` through the entry on every write, and the only things exercising it are tests.

That means the honest §3 answer isn't "bump to version 5" — there's nothing new to migrate, since the key is additive and always empty. It's the opposite question: **`members` is a mechanism with no remaining consumer.** Two ways to go:

- **Leave it.** It's inert and cheap, and something like per-member declarations may well return (#1493's credential-typed actions, or a future store/actuator split).
- **Remove it.** It's ~50 lines of validation and plumbing defending a shape nothing produces, and dead validation code tends to accumulate tests that pin behavior no user can reach.

I lean toward leaving it — the cost is low and the concept is likely to come back — but I'd flag it in #1480 as "landed, currently unused" rather than letting the issue keep implying a migration is owed. Noting that §4 is deferred to a major bump.

content.text:
You're right, and the code makes it sharper than "still representing a lock."

`VirtualLock` is dispatched on platform `"virtual"` — the hass-virtual custom integration — which creates a genuine `lock` domain entity. It has lock/unlock state, HA exposes lock/unlock services for it, and the tests drive it (`async_set(entity_id, "locked")`). LCM never actuates it, but "LCM doesn't use that half" isn't the same as "that half doesn't exist."

The decisive bit is what the provider says about itself:

```python
@property
def supports_code_slot_events(self) -> bool:
    """
    Return False: a virtual lock observes nothing.

    It is a recording surface -- somewhere to point a use that happened
    beyond Home Assistant's reach -- rather than a device that reports one.
    """
```

A keypad is *exactly* a thing that observes credential entry. This provider explicitly returns `False` for that. So against #1480's own three-role table:

| Role | `VirtualLock` |
|---|---|
| credential **store** | yes — its `Store` |
| credential **entry point** | **no** — observes nothing, by design |
| **actuated** thing | yes, a real lock entity; LCM just never drives it |

`VirtualKeypad` would name it after the single role it explicitly disclaims, and un-name the one role it genuinely has. The old note in #1480 said the rename "names the recording surface well" — that was wrong. A recording surface is where a use is *pointed*, not where it's *entered*; the entry point is the ESPHome keypad, which is the `source` on the event and isn't this provider at all.

So: **don't rename.** `VirtualLock` is accurate — it's a virtual lock that happens to be the credential store too. The store-not-device nature is already carried by the docstrings, the README row, and the wiki page, which is the right place for it.

Closes out #1480: **a provider is a credential store, not a lock.**

The headline change is that an entry can now manage **no locks at all**. Credentials live in the entry's configuration and are checked with `lock_code_manager.use_credential`, which is what a keypad Lock Code Manager cannot talk to actually needs — an entry to check credentials *against*, not a lock to write them *to*. That's issue #1414 (ESPHome keypads) and #1484.

Two designs were built and dropped on the way: a reader provider, then codeless-lock declarations (#1489). Both tried to give the keypad a lock-shaped identity. The working version doesn't: validation already reads the entry's own configuration, so the only thing standing in the way was availability being `any()` over the lock roster. ### What's in it

- **#1485** — `build_lock_instance` receives the config entry.
- **#1486 / #1500** — a per-member declaration shape, added for codeless locks and removed once that design was dropped. Net zero; they cancel out.

=== External-Keypads.md (     241 lines) ===
# External Keypads and Code Readers

Lock Code Manager can check a code entered somewhere it doesn't control — an
ESPHome keypad, a Wiegand reader, an intercom — against the users, PINs and
conditions you already configured, and record that the credential was used.

Because the check runs against the same users driving your real locks, one PIN
and one schedule cover both. Disable a user and their code stops working at the
keypad too.

Lock Code Manager never opens anything. It answers, records, and fires an event;
what happens next is yours.

## The action

```yaml
- action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
  data:
    config_entry_title: House Locks   # or config_entry_id
    code: "{{ entered_code }}"
    source: sensor.keypad_code        # where the code was entered
    target: lock.garage               # what it was used against
  response_variable: check
```

| Response | Value |
|---|---|
| `valid` | `true` / `false` |
| `user` | the user's name when valid, else `null` |
| `reason` | `unknown_code`, `user_disabled`, or `condition_not_met` when invalid |

`source` and `target` are both required and may be any entity. If you have no
natural entity for one, use a template entity as the source and a
[Virtual](https://github.com/twrecked/hass-virtual) lock as the target — see
[[Virtual integration|Virtual-integration]]. A keypad-only setup needs a Virtual
lock anyway, since a config entry requires at least one lock.

> **Don't name the same entity as both.** A use where `source` and `target` are
> equal is treated as one the lock observed by itself, and is not recorded again.

`reason` distinguishes a real-but-inactive credential from an unknown one, and
the action does no rate limiting or logging — so don't wire it to untrusted
input.

## What a valid code produces

**The `lock_code_manager_credential_used` event**, always:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the user |
| `config_entry_id`, `config_entry_title` | which configuration |
| `source` | where entered |
| `target` | what it was used against |

The same event fires when one of your locks reports a code used at its own
keypad, so a single trigger covers both.

**The user's `credential_used` event entity**, when `target` is a lock in that
config entry that can record events. Otherwise only the event fires — which is
normal for a keypad opening something LCM doesn't manage.

An invalid code produces nothing.

## Act on it

Import the **Credential Used** blueprint (see [[Blueprints]]): trigger on a
credential use, optionally filter by configuration, users, sources or targets,
and supply whatever actions you like — unlock a door, open a cover, start a
vacuum. Lock Code Manager needs to know nothing about what you're driving.

By hand:

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Garage: open on a valid keypad code"
    triggers:
      - trigger: event
        event_type: lock_code_manager_credential_used
        event_data:
          source: sensor.keypad_code
    actions:
      - action: cover.open_cover
        target: {entity_id: cover.garage_door}
```

## Security: keep the code out of your history

A keypad that publishes entered codes to an entity puts a cleartext PIN in that
entity's state, and the recorder keeps state history. Exclude it:

```yaml
recorder:
  exclude:
    entities:
      - sensor.keypad_code
```

Lock Code Manager never publishes that entity's state — only its entity ID. The
recorder is the one place it can't help, because the entity belongs to the
integration that publishes it.

Recipe 2 below avoids the entity entirely, which is the most private option.

---

# Recipes

### 1. Keypad entity → validate → open

On the device, publish the code and clear it (clearing is what lets the same
code be entered twice in a row):

```yaml
key_collector:
  - id: pin_collector
    source_id: keypad
    min_length: 4
    max_length: 8
    end_keys: "#"
    end_key_required: true
    on_result:
      - text_sensor.template.publish:
          id: keypad_code
          state: !lambda 'return x;'
      - delay: 1s
      - text_sensor.template.publish: {id: keypad_code, state: ""}
```

In Home Assistant:

```yaml
automation:
  - alias: "Garage: check keypad codes"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: sensor.keypad_code
        not_to: [unknown, unavailable, ""]
    actions:
      - action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
        data:
          config_entry_title: House Locks
          code: "{{ trigger.to_state.state }}"
          source: sensor.keypad_code
          target: lock.garage
        response_variable: check
      - if: "{{ check.valid }}"
        then:
          - action: cover.open_cover
            target: {entity_id: cover.garage_door}
```

> `not_to: [unknown, unavailable, ""]` is **not optional** — without it, a Wi-Fi
> reconnect that republishes the device's last value runs this with nobody at the
> keypad.

### 2. Let the keypad ask for itself

ESPHome 2025.10+ can capture an action's response, so the device decides locally
and the code never becomes an entity state at all.

```yaml
    on_result:
      - homeassistant.action:
          action: lock_code_manager.use_credential
          data_template:
            config_entry_title: House Locks
            code: "{{ entered }}"
            source: binary_sensor.garage_keypad_status
            target: lock.garage
          variables:
            entered: !lambda 'return x;'
          capture_response: true
          on_success:
            - if:
                condition:
                  lambda: 'return response["valid"].as<bool>();'
                then:
                  - switch.turn_on: garage_relay
                  - rtttl.play: "ok:d=4,o=5,b=100:c6"
                else:
                  - rtttl.play: "no:d=4,o=5,b=100:c4,c4"
```

`source` still has to name an entity — any entity belonging to the keypad will
do.

### 3. Different feedback per rejection reason

```yaml
      - choose:
          - conditions: "{{ check.valid }}"
            sequence:
              - action: tts.speak
                data: {message: "Welcome, {{ check.user }}."}
          - conditions: "{{ check.reason == 'condition_not_met' }}"
            sequence:
              - action: tts.speak
                data: {message: "That code isn't valid right now."}
          - conditions: "{{ check.reason == 'user_disabled' }}"
            sequence:
              - action: tts.speak
                data: {message: "That code has been turned off."}
        default:
          - action: tts.speak
            data: {message: "Code not recognized."}
```

### 4. A device that fires an event instead of publishing state

```yaml
    on_result:
      - homeassistant.event:
          event: esphome.keypad_code_entered   # must start with "esphome."
          data_template:
            code: "{{ entered }}"
          variables:
            entered: !lambda 'return x;'
```

Trigger on `esphome.keypad_code_entered` and pass
`trigger.event.data.code` to the action.

---

## Things to know

**PIN length is set by your strictest lock.** Every user's PIN must satisfy every
lock in the entry, so make `key_collector`'s bounds agree.

**Whitespace is ignored** on both stored PINs and submitted codes.

**Codes are matched as text** — nothing requires digits, though PINs are what
this is designed for.

**No rate limiting.** Brute-force defence belongs on the device; a keypad that
ignores input after several failures never troubles Home Assistant.

## See also

- [[Services and Actions]] · [[Blueprints]] · [[Virtual integration|Virtual-integration]]

The [Virtual](https://github.com/twrecked/hass-virtual) integration allows users to set up "virtual" entities of different types. One of those entity types is locks.

The reason support for this integration was added is because it can be used to test Lock Code Manager functionality without affecting your main locks. Because Virtual locks don't have support for setting and clearing user codes, the way this works is that user codes are persisted to disk as you set them. If you remove a Virtual lock from your configuration, the file will be removed to keep your file system clean.

If you are curious about Lock Code Manager and don't want to impact any existing locks functionality, I would encourage you to try setting up Lock Code Manager with Virtual locks first!

PS - the way Virtual locks integrate with LCM is not set in stone. If you have ideas on how to make support for these locks better, please open an issue.

## Anchoring a keypad-only setup

Virtual locks have a second use beyond trying things out. If you check codes
from an external keypad with `lock_code_manager.use_credential` and have no real
lock, add a Virtual lock to the config entry: it gives the entry slot capacity to
allocate against, somewhere for users and PINs to live, and an entity to name as
the `target` so uses are recorded on each user's credential used entity. See
[[External Keypads|External-Keypads]].

### Available Template Variables

Your condition template can use these variables:

| Variable | Description |

| `description` | Calendar event description |
| `location` | Calendar event location |

# Adding and Removing Locks

Each Lock Code Manager config entry manages a set of locks and a set of users. The user configuration applies to **every** lock in the entry, so adding or removing a lock changes which locks the entry's users are synced to — it does not change the user configuration itself.

All of the flows below start from **Settings → Devices & Services → Lock Code Manager**, then selecting the config entry.

## Adding a lock

1. Click **Configure** on the config entry.
2. Add the lock to the **Locks** selector.
3. Submit.

If the new lock already has codes programmed in slots that LCM will manage, a confirmation step lists them before anything is overwritten. Review it carefully — once confirmed, LCM will sync its configured users' PINs onto the lock.

## Removing a lock

1. Click **Configure** on the config entry.
2. Remove the lock from the **Locks** selector.
3. Submit.

LCM removes the entities it created for that lock and unlinks the lock's device from the config entry. The user configuration is untouched and continues to apply to the remaining locks.

> **⚠️ PINs are not cleared from the lock.** Removing a lock only stops LCM from managing it — any codes LCM programmed remain active on the physical lock. If you want them gone, disable the relevant users (or clear their PINs) **first**, wait for the lock to sync, and then remove the lock from the entry.

## Recovering when a lock entity was deleted outside LCM
